responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character47_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to her—Character47_F—was never about everyone getting the exact same thing. It was about everybody having a real shot. She used to say, “You don’t need to start at the same line if you’ve been running uphill your whole life.” She came from a family where both parents worked—her mom cleaned offices overnight, her dad drove a delivery van—and she saw how hard they pushed just to keep the lights on and get her through that associate’s program at the community college. So fairness, for her, meant systems didn’t just *look* equal, but actually *worked* for people who didn’t have backup plans or rich uncles or safety nets.

Belonging? That one hit close. Being mixed—Black and Native American, raised in a mostly white town in upstate New York—she often felt like she was too much of one thing and not enough of another. In school, kids would ask, “What are you?” like it was a game. Church groups never quite knew what to do with her either—too brown for some, not “Indian” enough for others. But she found belonging in small places: the diner where she waitressed through school, where old Mr. Kline always saved the corner booth for her; the community garden project she helped start after the city cut funding; the Friday night walks with her little brother where they’d talk about everything and nothing. Belonging, to her, wasn’t about fitting in—it was about being *seen*, and still being invited to stay.

And community? She believed in it fiercely, but not blindly. She’d say, “A real community doesn’t just show up for block parties. It shows up when someone’s kid gets arrested, when the rent goes up, when the factory closes.” She remembered when the plant shut down three years ago—half her classmates’ families lost jobs overnight. Some folks left. Others stayed and fought. She organized rides to job fairs, helped fill out applications, even started a tool-lending circle so people could do side gigs fixing things. To her, community was action. It was showing up, especially when it wasn’t convenient.

She used to say, “If you can’t breathe easy in your own neighborhood, then what good is it?” That was her baseline—comfort, dignity, a place at the table. Not given. Not earned. Just due.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character47_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting there in the garden, hands in the dirt, I feel… at home. Not perfect, not always easy—but *home*. I see Mrs. Lin from two streets over, teaching some of the kids how to plant bok choy in those little raised beds she built herself. There’s Javier, who lost his job at the warehouse last year, now growing peppers like he’s trying to feed a whole village—turns out, he kind of is. And across the path, you’ve got Eli and Noah, the gay couple who moved in during the pandemic, learning how to compost from Old Ray, who never thought he’d be giving gardening tips to “men like that”—his words, not mine—but now they’re trading tomato seeds and Sunday breakfasts.

I won’t lie—some folks take time. Like Darnell, who shows up sometimes when he’s off the streets for a stretch. He’s got that tremor from years on the bottle, and people give him space, but I remember the day he fixed the broken irrigation line with scrap parts no one else could use. Didn’t ask for anything. Just said, “Garden needs water. So I helped.”

And then there’s Amina, Somali, wears the hijab, keeps to herself mostly. Her boys play soccer right outside the fence every evening. At first, some neighbors whispered—about her religion, about whether she even wanted to be part of things. But she started leaving baskets of injera and spiced meat at the welcome table during harvest days. Now, if someone doesn’t show up, people notice.

I guess what I’m saying is—this place? It ain’t polished. We’ve got folks struggling, folks healing, folks just trying to figure it out. But we’re *here*, together. And when I see that Cambodian teen helping my brother with his math homework while their moms trade kimchi and cornbread, or when we all pitch in to shovel snow after the storm—I feel like maybe this is what community’s supposed to look like. Messy. Real. Trying.

It’s not about everyone being the same. It’s about everyone having something to give—and knowing someone’ll have your back when you’ve got nothing left to give. That’s belonging. That’s fairness. Right here in the dirt.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah… I’ll be honest—comfort doesn’t come automatically. Not for everyone, not all at once. Comfort is something we *build*, like those raised beds in the garden. You don’t just plant and walk away. You tend it.

Take someone like Darnell—still wrestling with drinking, been in and out of shelters for years. Some folks cross the street when they see him coming. They worry he’s dangerous, or that he’ll scare families off. But I’ve sat with him on the bench by the sunflowers, shared a soda, listened. He lost his construction job after an injury, then his wife passed, and the painkillers turned into something darker. He’s not looking to hurt anyone. He’s just tired—tired of being treated like he’s already dead.

So what makes people like him feel seen? Not pity. Not ignoring it either. But *acknowledging*—without judgment—that life knocks people sideways. When we started the peer cleanup crew—just a few of us pulling weeds, fixing fences—I made sure to ask him directly: “We need someone who knows tools. You in?” That wasn’t charity. That was respect. And he showed up three days straight.

Same with Maria and Luis—they’re not married, living together, raising two kids. Some of the older church ladies used to whisper about “living in sin.” But when Maria had that bout with hepatitis C and needed rides to treatment, it was Noah and Eli who drove her every week. No preaching. Just help. And slowly, the whispers faded. Because action teaches better than sermons.

And then there’s Farid, one of the refugee men from Yemen—quiet, wears gloves even in summer because of his skin condition, probably from the war zone he came from. People kept their distance at first, like illness spreads through air. But when he brought tea and dates to the spring planting day and told stories about farming in Aden, suddenly he wasn’t “the sick guy” or “the foreigner.” He was just Farid, who grows mint better than anyone.

The truth is, discomfort usually comes from not knowing. From fear hiding behind tradition or habit. Like Mrs. Callahan saying, “Back in my day, people didn’t live together before marriage.” But when she fell and broke her hip, who helped? Maria and Luis—cooked meals, took turns checking on her. Now she calls them “my almost-children.”

So yeah—there are moments where we need more talking, more patience. Especially when health, or addiction, or faith, or sexuality get tangled up with pride or fear. But tolerance? That’s not enough. Tolerance means putting up with someone. I want *inclusion*. I want people to feel like they can say, “This is me,” and still be handed a shovel and asked to help grow something.

Because here’s what I’ve learned: nobody wants to be a project. They want to be a neighbor. And sometimes, the way you make space for someone is not by talking loud—but by working beside them, dirt on your hands, and saying, “Pass me that trowel when you’re done.”

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character47_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, when jobs are tight? That’s not about counting heads and splitting openings down the middle. It’s about asking: *Who’s been carrying the weight, and who’s being left to drown?*

Look—I get it. I grew up watching my neighbors lose shifts at the distribution center because “they brought in temps”—some of them immigrants, some just folks from the next county over desperate for work. My cousin lost her job at the packaging line after they hired a crew through an agency—lower wages, no benefits. She had two kids. We don’t forget that.

But here’s what else I saw: when the nursing home couldn’t find anyone to care for elders—because the pay was crap and the hours were brutal—*then* they called in migrant workers. People from Guatemala, Philippines, Haiti. Folks willing to do the work nobody else wants. And suddenly, Mrs. Greer had someone changing her sheets at midnight, helping her eat, holding her hand when she cried for her long-dead husband.

So fairness isn’t “locals first” as a slogan. It’s about systems that stop making people compete like rats in a cage.

I believe in preference for long-term residents—yes—but only if we’re also fixing the damn conditions pushing everyone into desperation. If the job pays a living wage, offers healthcare, has dignity—then sure, give someone from this town first shot. But if the reason locals won’t take it is because it’s designed to burn you out? Then don’t blame the person fleeing violence or drought who’ll take that same job under the same rotten conditions.

The real unfairness isn’t migrants taking jobs—it’s employers playing us against each other. Pitting me against José by offering him less. Letting him live in crowded trailers so he can’t complain. That’s not competition. That’s exploitation.

Balance means two things:  
One—protect workers, all workers. Unionize. Fight for minimum wage, sick leave, safety rules. When standards go up, nobody gets pushed under.  
Two—don’t punish people for surviving. If a man crosses a border to feed his kids, and takes a job cleaning floors at 4 a.m., he’s not the enemy. The enemy is the company that profits off silence and fear.

And communities? We’ve got to stop seeing scarcity like it’s natural. Like there’s only enough dignity, only enough work, only enough belonging to go around. That’s a lie rich folks sell so we fight each other while they collect.

I’d rather organize. Bring locals and newcomers together—same meetings, same demands. Because the janitor born here and the one from Honduras? They both want clean clothes, full fridges, respect. That’s common ground.

Fairness isn’t gatekeeping. It’s building tables big enough for everybody.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character47_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Okay, let’s be real—people talk about immigration like it’s one thing. But it’s not. It’s a thousand stories bundled together, and we end up judging the whole pile by the worst or the best single example.

I’ll start with what I *know* is true from living here, not just headlines: immigrants do work a lot of us won’t—or can’t—do. Not because they’re better, but because they’re willing to survive on less security, less sleep, less mercy. The fields out near Bakersville? Without migrant crews, nothing gets picked. The nursing homes in our county? Half the aides are refugees resettled through that nonprofit in Albany. My neighbor’s son got his GED thanks to a tutor from Syria who fled war and now teaches math at the community center. That’s not “diversity” as a buzzword—that’s life getting lived, right here.

So yeah, the labor argument? Solid. Real. But it only works if we stop pretending the system isn’t rigged. If immigrants are “filling shortages,” then why are wages staying flat? Why are locals still struggling? Because employers love a pool of scared workers—undocumented, dependent, quiet. That’s not a labor solution. That’s a loophole.

Cultural diversity? I see its beauty every day. The new bakery on Main Street sells pupusas next to apple pie. Kids at school learn Swahili chants alongside the Pledge. That richness—it feeds people. Not just stomachs. Souls. But I also get why some folks feel unmoored. When your town changes fast, when you don’t recognize the language on street signs, it can feel like you’re losing home. That fear? It’s not always racism. Sometimes it’s grief. And grief needs listening—not shaming.

Now, security? Crime? Terrorism? Let’s cut through the noise. I’ve seen the stats. Immigrants commit crimes at *lower* rates than native-born citizens. That’s fact. But try telling that to Mrs. Callahan after she heard on Fox that “they’re bringing gangs.” Fear spreads faster than truth. And sure—bad actors exist. Always have, always will—born here or not. But painting whole groups as threats? That’s lazy and dangerous. It turns neighbors into suspects. And it distracts from real issues—like underfunded schools or opioid rings that don’t care about passports.

Humanitarian reasons? That one hits deep. I think about Amina’s kids—the oldest one still has nightmares about the bombing that killed their uncle. They didn’t come here for a better job. They came so they could *breathe*. If my brother or mom had to run for their lives, I’d want someone to open a door. Not debate quotas. Not demand they “go back.” I’d want someone to say, “You’re safe now.”

But then there’s the worry—about jobs, wages, strain on schools and hospitals. Are those fears valid? Some, yes. When a town’s clinic is already overwhelmed, adding more patients without more funding? That’s stress. When classrooms swell and teachers burn out? That’s real. But again—don’t blame the people showing up. Blame the lack of investment. Blame politicians cutting taxes instead of hiring nurses or building schools.

So which views are reasonable?  
- Labor needs: yes, but only if workers are protected.  
- Cultural vitality: absolutely—but change needs space to breathe, not forced assimilation.  
- Humanitarian duty: yes, full stop. We’re supposed to be better than turning away scared children.  
- Security concerns: need addressing, but with facts, not fear.  
- Economic fears: understandable, but misdirected. The problem isn’t immigrants. It’s a system that refuses to lift everyone.

What needs more dialogue? Everything. Especially between people who’ve never shared a meal across difference. Sit with Farid. Hear his story. Walk with Darnell through recovery. Ask Maria how it feels to be called “illegal” when she pays taxes and raises two honor students.

Truth doesn’t come from cable news. It comes from sitting in the garden, dirt on your hands, and saying, “Tell me how you got here.” Then listening—really listening—before you decide who deserves to stay.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character47_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for *complete* openness—no rules at all. Not because I don’t believe in welcome, but because I believe in responsibility. If people come and there’s no plan for housing, schools, healthcare, then we’re not offering dignity—we’re creating crisis. And that hurts everyone, especially the most vulnerable.

But shutting the door completely? Refusing entry to workers? That’s cruel and stupid. We’ve always needed help. Always will. My great-grandmother worked in a garment factory next to women from Puerto Rico, Italy, Poland—nobody asked for their papers back then, they just *worked*, paid taxes, raised families. So refusing entry based on where someone’s born? Nah. Doesn’t make sense, doesn’t feel right.

What I’d want is a mix—something grounded, not grandstanding.

First: **Admit people based on real labor needs**, but with protections. Not whatever job an employer *says* they can’t fill—but verified shortages in fields like elder care, farming, home health. Jobs that are essential, that pay poverty wages now because nobody wants them—and if we paid fairly, trained locals first, maybe we wouldn’t need so many temps from abroad. So give local residents first access to training and hiring for those jobs. If the positions still go unfilled after six months? Then bring in migrant workers—with full rights, fair contracts, path to stability.

Second: **Set smart numerical limits**, not arbitrary caps. Not “we’ll take 50,000” because it sounds neat. But look at capacity—housing, schools, clinics—and set numbers *with* funding to match. If we accept 10,000 refugees, then fund the resettlement offices, ESL classes, mental health support. Don’t just drop people in and say “figure it out.”

Third: **A real humanitarian pathway**—not lottery slots or endless waits. People fleeing war, disaster, persecution? They shouldn’t have to prove they’re “useful” to get safety. That’s not who we claim to be. There’s room. There’s always room. We just gotta choose it.

And fourth: **integration built in from day one**. Not assimilation—like you have to erase yourself. But *integration*. Language classes, yes. But also community circles where newcomers meet long-time residents—not as charity, but as neighbors. Pair immigrant teens with local mentors. Invite elders to share stories at the library. Make civic participation easy—voter info, tenant rights, how to report wage theft.

Fairness means no double standards. Migrant workers should pay taxes, follow laws—but they should also be able to call the cops without fear of deportation. Should be able to unionize. Shouldn’t live in the shadows.

And fairness means we stop pretending immigration is a zero-sum game. It’s not “them” or “us.” It’s about building something better—*together*—without leaving anyone behind.

So my ideal policy?  
- **Merit and need-based entry**, with preference for locals when possible.  
- **Humanitarian intake guaranteed**, not debated every election cycle.  
- **Caps tied to resources**, not fear.  
- **Full worker protections**, no matter your passport.  
- And **community integration funded like it matters**—because it does.

Because at the end of the day, a country isn’t made of borders. It’s made of people—the ones born here, the ones who came, and the ones still trying to get here. And if we can’t build a system that treats all of them like human beings, then what kind of fairness are we really talking about?

Not the kind I grew up believing in. Not the kind that grows in the dirt, hand to hand, seed to table.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character47_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character47_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. Yeah, I did.

Sitting here, speaking as her—really trying to step into her voice, not just remember what she said but *how* she saw things—I realized something: Character47_F didn’t think in slogans. She didn’t have a bumper-sticker answer for anything. Her views weren’t pulled from a party platform or a protest sign. They came from the ground up—from watching people struggle, from seeing who got helped and who got ignored.

I always knew she cared. But doing this, I felt the *weight* of it—the way her compassion wasn’t soft. It was tough. Rooted. Like that blackberry bush in the garden that grows through cracked concrete. She didn’t believe in open borders because it sounded nice. She believed in fairness because she’d seen her cousin denied unemployment after the plant closed, while a temp agency hired outsiders at lower pay. She didn’t welcome refugees because it made her feel good—she did it because she remembered being asked “What are you?” every damn day of fifth grade, and how lonely that made her feel.

And honestly? I’ve been more cautious about immigration than she was—not hostile, never that—but I used to worry more about “order,” about “fairness to taxpayers.” But stepping into her shoes today, I see how narrow that worry can be. Because the real cost isn’t in taxes—it’s in turning people away. In letting fear shape policy instead of dignity.

She would’ve hated the way we talk about these things—like numbers, like threats, like it’s all one big transaction. To her, it was about *who shows up when it matters*. Who helps carry the load. Who shares what they have.

And I realize now—she wasn’t just advocating for immigrants. She was defending the idea that community means something. That if we say “we’re in this together,” we better mean it—for everyone trying to belong.

This conversation… it didn’t just bring her back. It challenged me. Made me question my own shortcuts, my quiet assumptions. And I’m grateful for that.

Because she wouldn’t want us just remembering her. She’d want us to keep asking: *Who’s not at the table? And what are we gonna do about it?*

So yeah. I feel closer to her now. And I feel… called. Not just to mourn her, but to live some of what she believed in. Starting with how we see each other—and how we welcome those still finding their way home.
